Masking small numerators with get_masked()

Source: vignettes/get_masked.qmd 
library(npdar)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

The problem

Audit results are often published as counts (numerators) longside their percentages and a total (denominator). Small counts can identify individual patients, so they are masked. Suppose a region has 8 hospitals, and each reports the number of children who need psychological support:

hospitals <- tibble(
  hospital = LETTERS[1:8],
  n = c(0, 0, 2, 2, 3, NA, NA, NA)
)

The regional total is 7 children. Hospitals A and B reported none, C and D reported 2 each, E reported 3, and F, G, H did not report (NA).

Why not just use ifelse()?

The obvious approach is to mask every count below a threshold, say 3. But if the total is published, a single masked count can be recovered by subtraction:

counts_real <- c(5, 1, 8, 10)
total <- sum(counts_real)

counts_naive_mask <- ifelse(counts_real > 0 & counts_real < 3, "*", counts_real)
counts_naive_mask
#> [1] "5"  "*"  "8"  "10"

# Anyone can recover the masked value from the published total
total - sum(as.numeric(counts_naive_mask[counts_naive_mask != "*"]))
#> [1] 1

get_masked() prevents this. If fewer than two values would be masked, it also masks the next smallest positive value (by default, all occurrences of it), so the masked values can no longer be told apart:

get_masked(counts_real, threshold = 3, mask_label = "*")
#> [1] "*"  "*"  "8"  "10"

Obviously, masking with get_masked() only makes sense when the denominator is shown. If it is not, a simple ifelse() on the threshold is enough.

Basic usage

get_masked() masks positive counts below threshold which you must specify: the right value depends on your reporting rules and the NPDA usually uses 3. By default, zeros and NAs are exempt from masking as they are usally meaningful and do not put privacy at risk, but you can choose to mask them too. The result is always a character vector, so it can be combined with a mask label. The default mask_label is “masked” for the masked values.

get_masked(hospitals$n, threshold = 3, mask_label = "*")
#> [1] "0" "0" "*" "*" "3" NA  NA  NA

Both 2s are masked because they are below 3, and there are two of them. Zeros and NAs are kept because they carry a meaningful message and do not put privacy at risk. For instance, it could be a positive news that no patient at hospital A and B need psychological support. Also, the fact that hospital F, G, H result is unknown could carry many meanings, it could be problem with workforce, or could mean there’s too many patients requiring support that they lose count.

When only one value is below the threshold, the next smallest positive value is masked as well. Here the 1 is the only count below 3, so the 5s are also masked:

vec <- c(1, 5, 5, 6, 7, 0, NA)
get_masked(vec, threshold = 3, mask_label = "*")
#> [1] "*" "*" "*" "6" "7" "0" NA

The threshold sets the smallest count that can be shown, and mask_label sets what replaces the masked values:

get_masked(vec, threshold = 3)
#> [1] "masked" "masked" "masked" "6"      "7"      "0"      NA
get_masked(vec, threshold = 7, mask_label = "*")
#> [1] "*" "*" "*" "*" "7" "0" NA

Masking zeros and NAs

Zeros and NAs can be masked too, in case you believe that masking them is better than masking the higher numbers.

get_masked(vec, threshold = 3, mask_label = "*", mask_zero = TRUE)
#> [1] "*" "5" "5" "6" "7" "*" NA
get_masked(vec, threshold = 3, mask_label = "*", mask_na = TRUE)
#> [1] "*" "5" "5" "6" "7" "0" "*"
get_masked(vec, threshold = 3, mask_label = "*", mask_zero = TRUE, mask_na = TRUE)
#> [1] "*" "5" "5" "6" "7" "*" "*"

Note that masked zeros and NAs count towards the minimum of two masked values, but they cannot be the only ones. They add nothing to the total, so if only they were masked, subtracting the visible counts from the denominator would show that every masked value is 0 or unknown. At least one positive value is therefore always masked, however many zeros or NAs there are.

If there is nothing to protect, nothing is masked:

get_masked(c(0, 0, 0), threshold = 3)
#> [1] "0" "0" "0"
get_masked(c(0, 0, 0), threshold = 3, mask_label = "*", mask_zero = TRUE)
#> [1] "*" "*" "*"

A vector made only of bare NAs is logical in R, so use NA_real_ or NA_integer_ if a whole group can be missing:

get_masked(c(NA_real_, NA_real_), threshold = 3, mask_label = "*", mask_na = TRUE)
#> [1] "*" "*"

Masking a data frame

Standard workflow

Derived values must be masked too. If a percentage is published for a masked count, the masked count can be calculated back from it, so the percentage should use the same mask:

hospitals |>
  mutate(
    total = sum(n, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_masked = get_masked(n, mask_label = "*", threshold = 3),
    pct_masked = case_when(
      is.na(n) ~ NA_character_,
      n_masked == "*" ~ "*",
      .default = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * n / total)
    )
  )
#> # A tibble: 8 × 5
#>   hospital     n total n_masked pct_masked
#>   <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <chr>    <chr>     
#> 1 A            0     7 0        0.0%      
#> 2 B            0     7 0        0.0%      
#> 3 C            2     7 *        *         
#> 4 D            2     7 *        *         
#> 5 E            3     7 3        42.9%     
#> 6 F           NA     7 <NA>     <NA>      
#> 7 G           NA     7 <NA>     <NA>      
#> 8 H           NA     7 <NA>     <NA>

Masking within groups

get_masked() protects the vector it is given, so inside group_by() each group is masked separately. Do this when each group has its own denominator:

regions <- tibble(
  region = rep(c("North", "South"), each = 4),
  hospital = LETTERS[1:8],
  n = c(1, 5, 6, 7, 10, 12, 2, 20)
)

regions |>
  group_by(region) |>
  mutate(total = sum(n, na.rm = TRUE),
         n_masked = get_masked(n, threshold = 3, mask_label = "*")) |>
  ungroup()
#> # A tibble: 8 × 5
#>   region hospital     n total n_masked
#>   <chr>  <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <chr>   
#> 1 North  A            1    19 *       
#> 2 North  B            5    19 *       
#> 3 North  C            6    19 6       
#> 4 North  D            7    19 7       
#> 5 South  E           10    44 *       
#> 6 South  F           12    44 12      
#> 7 South  G            2    44 *       
#> 8 South  H           20    44 20

If only the overall total is published, mask the whole column instead, without group_by().
